summary: Lists the goals for SMIng, a proposed new data definition language for modeling network management information that could map to SNMP and COPS-PR operations. It sets objectives rather than defining the language itself. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP has its own language for describing managed objects, and policy provisioning has another that is almost the same but not quite. This memo lists the goals for a single language that would replace both, along with the features it must have and the mappings that would let it feed SNMP and COPS-PR.

questions: what was smi next generation meant to do
subtitle: Design objectives for a single data definition language for network management, replacing SMIv2 and SPPI.

tldr.problem: Network management data is written in several incompatible languages: SMIv2 for SNMP, SPPI for policy, and other schemes elsewhere, so the same idea has to be described again for each.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the objectives a new language, SMIng, has to meet: one core document, a textual syntax people can read and write, a rigorous grammar, namespace control, the SMIv2 and SPPI base types, and a mapping to SNMP and COPS-PR. Each objective is tagged by type and by origin.
tldr.outcome: The objectives are grouped as accepted, nice-to-have and rejected. The memo is Informational and sets goals rather than defining the language.

today: RFC 3216 is an Informational memo listing the objectives for SMIng, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It sets goals rather than defining a language, and says the language itself has no security impact on the Internet. The two languages it set out to merge are RFC 2578 for SMIv2 and RFC 3159 for SPPI.

sections.title: What the Memo Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
The memo describes the objectives for a new data definition language that can be mapped into SNMP and COPS-PR protocol operations, and which may also be translated into SMIv2 MIBs and SPPI PIBs. Concepts such as attributes, attribute groups, methods, conventions for organizing reusable data structures and mechanisms for representing relationships are discussed. Its purpose is to serve as a set of objectives that a subsequent language specification should try to address, and it captures the results of the working group's discussions towards consensus.

The objectives are organized into three groups: accepted objectives, nice-to-have objectives and rejected objectives. Each objective carries a type and an origin. The type says what kind of objective it is. Basic means it is contained in SMIv2 or SPPI. Align means SMIv2 and SPPI support it in different ways and they must be aligned. Fix means it addresses a known problem in SMIv2 or SPPI. New means it is a new feature. The origin says where it comes from: SMI, SPPI, the NMRG proposal, the working group charter, or proposed during working group discussions. Each objective then has a description, a motivation and optional notes, which for the nice-to-have and rejected objectives may explain why the working group did not require it, while still saying why it should be considered anyway. The notes are the opinions of the participants in the discussion and are not to be taken as the consensus of the working group.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not define a language. It lists what any such language should do, and marks each item so a reader can see whether it is something already in use, a fix for a known fault, or something new, and where the idea came from.

sections.title: Why One Language
sections.content:
As networking technology has evolved, a diverse set of technologies has been deployed to manage the resulting products, from Web-based products to standard management protocols and text scripts. The systems being managed are represented in varying ways: implicitly in the system programming, through proprietary data descriptions, or with standardized descriptions using a range of technologies including MIBs, PIBs and LDAP schemas. The result is that management interfaces for network protocols, services and applications such as Differentiated Services may be represented in many different and inconsistent fashions.

The SMIng working group has been chartered to define a new data definition language that will eliminate the need for a separate SMIv2 and SPPI language, so that the new language addresses the needs of the current SMIv2 and SPPI languages and over time they can all be replaced by it.

Another motivation is to permit a more expressive and complete representation of the modeled information. The examples given are the ability to formally define table existence relationships, the expression of instance creation and deletion capabilities, and the ability to define attribute groups using inheritance.

The working group has also recognized that merging SMIv2 and SPPI on the one hand, and enhancing the state of the art in management data modelling on the other, can lead to conflicts. Where they do, the consensus is to focus on enhancing the state of the art in network management data modelling.
sections.plainLanguage: Today the same kind of management information may be described in several ways, depending on which protocol carries it. One language would mean writing it once, and it would also let the language say things the older ones cannot, such as when a row must exist.

sections.title: Where the Proposal Came From
sections.content:
The Network Management Research Group of the IRTF researched the issues of creating a protocol-independent data definition language that could be used by multiple protocols. Because SMIv2 and SPPI are very similar, the NMRG focused on merging those two, but also researched ways to abstract the objectives to produce a language that could be used for other protocols such as LDAP and Diameter. It published its results in an Internet Draft that has since expired, and submitted its specification as one proposal for consideration in the development of the SMIng language.

The SMIng working group accepted that submission for consideration, and uses it to better understand the objectives and the possible obstacles to be overcome. Where useful, the NMRG proposal is referenced in the details of the objectives.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the working group started, a research group had already tried to write the merge-up as a draft specification. The working group took that draft as a starting point for working out what it actually wanted.

sections.title: The Accepted Objectives
sections.content:
The accepted objectives are the ones the working group found worthwhile and deserving of further consideration. Each of them must still be evaluated to decide whether the benefit justifies the cost, and an accepted objective may later be rejected if it conflicts with another objective considered more important. The list runs to more than forty items, and the following are the ones that shape the language most.

On the shape of the specification: the core of SMIng must be defined in one document and must be independent of external specifications, because SMIv2 is defined in three documents based on an obsolete ITU ASN.1 specification while SPPI is defined in one. Definitions must be represented in a textual format, and the syntax must make it easy for humans to read and write modules, so that module authors can produce them with ordinary text editing tools. There must be a rigorously defined syntax, because an unambiguous language promotes consistency across vendors so that different parsers produce the same results.

On naming: SMIng must provide mechanisms to uniquely identify attributes, groups of attributes and events, and must say how name collisions are handled. There must be a hierarchical, centrally-controlled namespace for standard named items, and a distributed namespace to allow vendor-specific naming and to assure unique module names across vendors, because some SMI implementations have problems with different objects from multiple modules sharing a name, and the probability of module name clashes rises over time. Modules need a mechanism for unique identification and for stating status, contact person, revision information and purpose, and for detailing the minimum requirements an implementer must meet to claim conformance. The language must have characteristics so that future modules can contain information of future syntax without breaking original parsers, and it must allow an escaping mechanism for special characters in text such as descriptions and references, because ABNF can contain literal characters in double quotes.

On data: SMIng must support the base data types Integer32, Unsigned32, Integer64, Unsigned64, Enumeration, Bits, OctetString and OID, with Counter and Gauge regarded as derived types rather than base types, and the list of base types must not be extensible unless SMI itself changes. It must support a mechanism to derive new types that carry additional semantics, such as counters, gauges and strings, and new types must be as restrictive or more restrictive than the types they specialize. It must support enumerations, with enumerated values part of the enumeration definition, and discriminated unions, which allow related attributes to be grouped together, such as InetAddressType as the discriminator with InetAddress, InetAddressIPv4 and InetAddressIPv6 as the union.

On structure: an attribute group is a named, reusable set of attributes that are meaningful together and can be reused as the type of attributes in other attribute groups, which the memo compares to structs in C. SMIng must support creating new attribute groups from attributes of more basic types and from other attribute groups, and must support single inheritance and both reusable and final attribute groups. It must support the table existence relationships INDEX, AUGMENTS and EXTENDS, and also EXPANDS and REORDERS, where a REORDERS statement allows indexing orders to be swapped and an EXPANDS statement formally states a one-to-many existence relationship between table rows.

On pointers and rules: SMIng must allow specifying pointers to instances and pointers to rows, and must allow specifying the types of objects to which a pointer may point, which lets code generators detect and reject illegal pointers automatically. It must support events identifying significant state changes, creation and deletion operations for instances with specific errors such as INSTALL-ERRORS, range and size constraints, uniqueness constraints on attributes including multiple independent ones, extension rules, and a deprecation of the IMPLIED keyword. The definitions themselves must be protocol independent, so that the same data can be used with multiple protocols and multiple versions of them, while the working group defines the mappings to SNMP and COPS-PR. Constructs must, wherever possible, be translatable to SMIv2 and SPPI, and existing SMIv2 MIBs and SPPI PIBs on the standards track will not be required to be translated, while new MIBs and PIBs will be defined in the new language.
sections.plainLanguage: The accepted list is long. The important themes are: one self-contained document, text a person can type, a grammar strict enough that two parsers agree, names that cannot collide, the same base types the older languages use, reusable groups of attributes, ways of saying that one row implies another, and a mapping layer that turns the definitions into SNMP or COPS-PR operations.

sections.title: Nice-to-Have and Rejected Objectives
sections.content:
The nice-to-have objectives are recommended but are not automatically accepted, because they may entail a non-trivial amount of work in the underlying protocols to support them, or may be regarded as less important than other accepted objectives that contradict them. They include methods, that is, a mechanism to define method signatures with parameters, return values and exceptions, which are needed for operational interfaces such as ping, traceroute and lookup, and which could also address problems such as those encountered with SNMP's RowStatus solution. There is disagreement about the impact: one end of the spectrum sees methods as a documentation tool for existing SNMP capabilities, the other sees them as a protocol update, and the proposal is to wait and see whether methods can be implemented as a syntax that is useful and can map to the protocol. The others include unions, float data types, comments, referencing tagged rows, arrays, internationalization, and separating data modelling from management protocol mapping.

The rejected objectives are the ones the working group decided not to pursue. Rejecting an objective does not mean it must not be addressed. Among them are incomplete translations, where not all information in the new language may be directly translatable to a MIB or PIB construct, with the memo's own summary of that section reading that reality sucks and all information should at least be conveyed in documentation or by other means. Others are attribute value constraints between the values of multiple attributes, attribute transaction constraints, method constraints, agent capabilities, relationships, procedures, associations and association cardinalities, categories of modules, mapping modules to files, a simple grammar, the place of module information, module namespace, and hyphens in identifiers.

On the last of these the memo notes the confusion about whether hyphens are allowed in SMIv2 identifiers, since module names may contain them, node identifiers usually do not, and identifiers such as mib-2 do because of their SMIv1 origin. It says SMIng should simply allow hyphens in all kinds of identifiers, while noting that compilers mapping SMIng to programming languages have to quote hyphens where a hyphen would otherwise be read as a minus.
sections.plainLanguage: The nice-to-have list holds features the group liked but could not justify. The rejected list holds features it decided against, with the reasoning recorded so a later reader can disagree with the decision and see what it would cost to change it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it defines objectives for a language with which to write and read descriptions of management information, and that the language itself has no security impact on the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: A language for writing descriptions does not change what the described systems do, so the memo says it raises no security questions of its own.
